COP31 talks face early friction over future of fossil fuels

ANTALYA: Big fossil fuel producers and consumers at the COP31 climate talks are resisting any deal that would specify firm new targets or a shift away from oil, gas and coal , observers said on Friday (Nov 13) as the first week of talks drew to a close. That poses a challenge for summit host Türkiye and lead negotiator Australia, which has another week to land the kind of ambitious agreement climate advocates say is needed to address the worsening impacts of global warming. "Positions are still quite entrenched in terms of where they are, but that's pretty normal at this stage," said Cosima Cassel, an observer to the talks from environmental group E3G. Major oil producers such as Saudi Arabia and Russia have traditionally resisted language constraining fossil fuels , while large developing economies such as India have opposed measures they say could limit their development and energy choices, a dynamic that has compromised the outcomes of past deals.

The world’s biggest oil consumer, the United States, meanwhile, has skipped the talks for the second year in a row under US President Donald Trump, who has called global warming a hoax and promoted continued use of fossil fuels . The stance is at odds with the increasing severity of global warming, scientists and campaigners say. A UN report last month found the world is on course to exceed the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warming limit that countries had agreed to pursue under the 2015 Paris Agreement to prevent the worst effects of climate change. As temperatures have risen, this year has been marked by extreme heatwaves across Western Europe and a glacier collapse in Nepal that triggered a flood that killed more than 1,450 people. Thousands more are still missing.

ELECTRIFICATION AND NO FIRM TARGETS COP31 host Turkey is striving to place a proposal to expand global electrification at the centre of an eventual deal, saying the plan will lead to emissions cuts by speeding the shift away from fossil fuel-powered cars, boilers and other equipment. The proposal does not require the increased electricity use come from renewable sources, although some countries, including last year’s COP host Brazil, are advocating for progress on a plan to require countries to more cl early map out their transition away from fossil fuels . Katrine Petersen, another E3G observer, said whether those measures survive the talks depends on conversations in the days to come. "We've also heard quite cl early from countries like India, the G77, that they don't want any firm targets. They don't want any kind of technology or fuel-specific language," she said. "(These are) the kind of consistent and ongoing divides that we've seen from those different parties before." Representatives from India, Saudi Arabia and Russia did not immediately comment.

Related:

Diana Acconcia, head of the EU delegation, said Europe backed the electrification goal. "Electrification is, in a way, an inclusive agenda because it is non-prescriptive in a way on how the electrification is achieved," she said. "Of course, for the European Union electrification is to be achieved by clean sources of energy." The Australian team, which is leading negotiations under a split presidency arrangement, spent the first few days of the summit gathering views on what should be included in a political text agreed by consensus that will be followed by all the negotiated technical points. Australia is taking further submissions from countries until Saturday night, with a view to formulating a draft text early next week.

Source: Reuters/fs

FAST

LONDON: Old-school technology including telephones, faxes and Bluetooth limited the damage for some people on Friday (Nov 13) as a worldwide outage of Microsoft's Outlook left millions without email. The prolonged disruption, which also hit Microsoft Teams and Copilot, affected some of the world's biggest institutions, from bankers and traders to shipping firms. While most reported their core systems were still running, trading and administrative work slowed in places in the latest reminder of how much of the world's commerce, public services and communications run on a handful of technology providers. "The pressure is mounting to invest in contingency plans and test whether those backups actually work when needed," said PP Foresight analyst Paolo Pescatore, adding that firms needed multiple providers for key services like communication and data storage.

Microsoft, which says on its website that more than 430 million people use its 365 services, blamed server problems and said it was not aware of any malicious activity.  The disruption comes weeks after attacks on the industrial systems that keep supermarket food cold and shows how a single point of failure, whether a technical fault, cyberattack or even an extreme weather event, can disrupt everyday business. In its latest update on Friday, Microsoft said it was seeing signs of stabilisation after implementing fixes more broadly to attain a persistent recovery of services.

Related:

European exchange operator Euronext, which runs bourses in Paris, Brussels, Lisbon, Amsterdam, Oslo, Athens and Milan, told listed companies to pick up the phone. "We have ensured that the team has sufficient capacity to manage the situation and handle the additional workload," a spokesperson said, adding that Euronext was verifying the identity of callers to protect confidentiality and integrity. Aviva, which reported earnings on Friday, said it had put backup plans in place, including sending out alternative phone numbers for earnings calls and using Bluetooth to transfer recordings because email was down. The British insurer tested a similar-scale outage of its most critical technology systems about two weeks ago, CEO Amanda Blanc told Reuters.  Shipping group Maersk asked customers to call with anything urgent and urged them to verify any unexpected communications about the outage with their local representative.

Related:

What the Microsoft Outlook outage reveals about risks, limitations and gaps in communication

FAX MACHINES RETURN IN TAIPEI In Taiwan, the outage disrupted fund management at securities firms, life insurers and investment trust companies, people familiar with the situation said. At another financial firm, trades such as purchases and sales of short-term bills, which are normally confirmed by email, had to be confirmed by fax instead, one of the people said. Foreign banks and financial institutions in Taiwan were hit especially hard, a trader said, because much of their data is emailed to overseas headquarters through Microsoft's systems. In Britain, HSBC and Barclays activated internal incident teams to assess the impact, people within the banks told Reuters. While email systems were down, most client services were unaffected. HSBC reminded staff not to use unauthorised channels such as personal email or WhatsApp to get around the outage, one said. Two trading professionals said they observed lower trading volumes in some markets on Friday that they attributed to difficulties in executing trades.  Caitlin Egen of Control Risks said that big global firms usually had contingency plans, but when key services went down abruptly, it was still a "wake-up call". "For a lot of businesses this morning, it's probably been chaos trying to figure out how to even get in touch with people," she said.

Source: Reuters/rk

Europe must show it is ready to contribute to the Ukraine peace process before a decision is made on letting Europeans join the negotiations, the Kremlin said on Friday (Nov 13).

MOSCOW: The Kremlin said on Friday (Nov 13) that Europe must show it is ready to contribute to the Ukraine peace process before a decision is made on letting Europeans join the negotiations. The comment by Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov suggests Russia has not yet committed to including Europeans in the next round of talks, despite US negotiators saying on Thursday that President Vladimir Putin had agreed to their participation. The talks have so far involved Russian, Ukrainian and US officials, who met in Abu Dhabi this week for the first time in nine months. Two US envoys then flew to Moscow to meet Putin and later met Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy in Dublin. Asked if peace talks would soon resume with the added participation of Europeans, Peskov said: "Once we understand their genuine intention and readiness to contribute to the peace process, then it will be possible to make a decision on holding dialogue on a Ukrainian settlement in an expanded format."

European involvement would mark a new phase in efforts to end the nearly five-year-old conflict, which has defied attempts by US President Donald Trump to secure a peace agreement.

Related:

Germany's Merz asks Trump for 'no surprises' from Putin talks

Russia's relations with European powers are dire. European states have armed Ukraine and imposed sanctions on Moscow, and most have shunned direct contact with Putin since he sent troops to Ukraine in February 2022. Putin said on Thursday the US must work with its European allies to understand whether they wanted peace or war in Ukraine. Peskov said Moscow would be open to the idea of some form of contacts with Europe before any European participation in peace negotiations, but that no concrete discussions on this had taken place. Asked how the Kremlin would view French President Emmanuel Macron as a potential interlocutor at peace talks, Peskov said: "Every hour, reports are appearing that name completely different candidates. So for the time being we are not in a position to say anything specific." WHO WOULD REPRESENT EU? Peskov declined to comment on the possibility of European Union foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas representing the EU at negotiations. Kallas has frequently questioned Russia's good faith in the peace process and taken a lead in imposing successive waves of sanctions on Moscow. She said on Friday it was not up to Russia to say who should represent the EU in peace talks. "They don't want anybody strong on the other side because they want to push through their maximum demands," she said. Russia says it wants a full peace settlement, not a ceasefire. Foreign Minister Sergei Lavrov said this week that Moscow wanted to negotiate a broad European security framework before tackling the specifics of the war. Russian and Ukrainian officials said some progress was made at the Abu Dhabi talks, but there was no sign of a major breakthrough on key issues such as territory. Putin has shown no signs of being ready to moderate his territorial demands, which include a buffer zone in parts of Ukraine which Russia has not formally claimed as its own. Ukraine has refused Russia's demands to give up territory in the eastern Ukrainian region of Donbas that it has not lost in fighting.

Source: Reuters/ht

BERLIN: German Chancellor Friedrich Merz on Friday (Nov 13) urged US President Donald Trump not to spring any surprises during expected talks on Ukraine with Russian President Vladimir Putin in China next week. "Some here in Dublin fear this could turn into a 'second Anchorage moment'," said Merz, referring to the Trump-Putin summit in Anchorage, Alaska, that European leaders had viewed as a potentially pivotal moment in efforts to end the war in Ukraine. "I therefore want to state our message to the United States very clearly: please, no surprises. Continue to play as part of 'Team Europe' and 'Team Ukraine'." Merz is pushing for EU leaders to commit to supporting Ukraine as part of negotiations on the bloc's long-term budget.

VIENNA: The UN nuclear watchdog is "increasingly concerned" about a uranium-enrichment plant at Isfahan that Iran declared to it last year but has still not let the watchdog inspect, it said in a confidential report on Iran on Friday (Nov 13) seen by Reuters. Iran has not let International Atomic Energy Agency (IAEA) inspectors return to any of its nuclear facilities bombed by Israel and the United States in a 12-day campaign in June last year that destroyed or badly damaged Iran's other uranium enrichment plants, the heart of its nuclear programme. The targets included a tunnel network at Isfahan where diplomats have said they believe the Isfahan Fuel Enrichment Plant (IFEP) - declared to the agency on Jun 12, 2025 - is located, though a senior diplomat said that its whereabouts and status remained unknown. The IAEA had planned to inspect the plant on Jun 13, 2025 but the bombing campaign started that day, making it impossible.

IAEA chief Rafael Grossi said in March his agency believed a significant amount of Iran's most highly enriched uranium was in the tunnel complex at Isfahan. While the report singled out IFEP, it also reiterated that Iran should inform the IAEA of the status of its enrichment plants as well as its stock of highly enriched uranium, which includes material close to weapons grade, and let inspectors return to the bombed sites and account for the enriched uranium. "The Agency's lack of information about this nuclear material and access to facilities to verify it is a matter of serious proliferation concern .... and needs to be rectified with the utmost urgency," it said.

SYDNEY: Australia's spy agency and federal police were among organisations caught up in an outage of Microsoft programmes on Friday (Nov 13), with the government triggering an agreement to ensure priority restoration of services. Users worldwide have been unable to access services for hours, including Microsoft 365, Outlook and Teams. At a news conference, Australian Security Intelligence Organisation Director-General Mike Burgess and Australian Federal Police Commissioner Krissy Barrett confirmed their organisations have been affected. Home Affairs Minister Tony Burke said Microsoft told him it did not believe the outage was caused by a cyber attack. The government has activated an agreement to ensure Australia gets prioritised in restoring services, Burke said. "There is good security work that is done with Microsoft as a business and when it came to the formal cyber agreements which I've signed on behalf of Australia, the first of those was with Microsoft," Burke said at the news conference. "That agreement has in fact been activated today to make sure that we get appropriate prioritisation of Australian interests in this".

WASHINGTON: United States House Speaker Mike Johnson said on Thursday (Nov 12) there was growing consensus in Congress on limiting chip exports to China after a spy scandal forced out Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang . Huang stepped down after reports of a romantic relationship with a businesswoman whom US authorities suspect of spying for the Chinese government.  Lawmakers from both parties have since called for tougher restrictions on China's access to advanced artificial intelligence chips, threatening access to chips that underpin China's surging AI development. Nvidia's advanced AI chips are widely used to develop cutting-edge AI models, making the company key to the US race against China to build superior AI systems. The US has sought for years to limit China’s access to Nvidia’s chips because it does not want the Chinese military to benefit from them.

"The export controls on chips to China has been a big issue around here," Johnson, a Louisiana Republican, told reporters at the US Capitol, adding he favoured limiting China's access to the advanced technology.  "I think there's a developing consensus in Congress that is an important position to take." The Chinese businesswoman, Alice Huang, was an executive at Megaspeed , an Nvidia partner the US government suspects of helping China obtain advanced AI chips restricted under US export controls. Beijing has denied Alice Huang is a spy.

Related:

Who is Alice Huang, Chinese exec accused of spying on Nvidia CEO?

Commentary: Everything Jensen Huang said about China is out the window

REPUBLICANS EYE EXPORT RESTRICTIONS The case has revived claims among China critics in Washington that US export policies are too weak, boosting calls for more restrictions. Reuters reported that Chinese AI companies are trying to rent Nvidia-powered computing capacity outside China because they are worried the Jensen Huang allegations could spur Washington to tighten restrictions on their ability to access the company's chips remotely.   Congressional Republicans are keen to attach new restrictions on exporting advanced AI chips to China in the annual defence authorisation Bill, a must-pass measure that funds the military and typically attracts bipartisan support, according to a Senate aide, who spoke on the condition of anonymity.  Lawmakers are pressing their colleagues to pass at least four Bills on chip exports, according to statements since Monday.  The AI Overwatch Act would give Congress more power over advanced AI chip exports. The Chip Security Act would require companies to track the location of advanced AI processors to prevent smuggling.  The Match Act would pressure US allies to restrict sales and maintenance of advanced chipmaking equipment destined for China. The Remote Access Security Act would give the Commerce Department the tools to stop Chinese firms from renting overseas data centres to access Nvidia chips. Jensen Huang is separately expected to testify before Congress before Thanksgiving, which falls on Nov 26.  House Foreign Affairs Chairman Brian Mast, a Florida Republican, told reporters on Thursday that congressional staff spoke with Nvidia on Wednesday night about a date and location for his testimony.  Mast and two other leading House Republicans asked Huang last week to brief them behind closed doors about his relationship with the suspected Chinese spy.

ANTALYA: World leaders have set out competing positions and made clashing demands in two days of intense speech-making at the COP31 climate change talks in Türkiye , leaving negotiators with a tough task to draft a meaningful deal that all can agree. Small island states, among the most vulnerable in the world as global warming makes sea levels rise, pleaded for urgent cuts to greenhouse gas emissions. European leaders , meanwhile, lined up behind a proposal to expand global electrification, developing countries asked for more finance from rich ones, and fossil fuel producers said oil, gas, and coal should continue to be used. "We reaffirm our sovereign right to strengthen our energy and oil industry as a driver of our national development," Venezuela's acting President Delcy Rodriguez told the conference, after UN leaders had made the case for bringing to an end the age of fossil fuel.

Apart from trying to accommodate incompatible national positions aired on Wednesday (Nov 11) and Thursday (Nov 12), conference host Türkiye and negotiations lead Australia also have the challenge of trying to make progress when wars and inflation have pushed climate concerns down the political agenda. "It's my job to steer consensus, not to bang tables and demand any particular action, but to steer consensus to the strongest , most ambitious possible out come within the constraints of that consensus-driven process," Chris Bowen, Australia's COP31 president of negotiations , told Reuters. Asked what a good deal might look like, he said: "I have many more hours of consultations with partners to do." Climate activists say short-term political concerns should not get in the way of addressing an issue that will get more pressing if ignored. A UN report last month found the world was already on course to break through the 1.5 degrees Celsius (2.7 degrees Fahrenheit) warming limit that countries had agreed to pursue under the 2015 Paris Agreement to prevent the worst effects of climate change. "The situation could not be less under control. The planet is not dying. It is being killed," Swedish climate activist Greta Thunberg said on the sidelines of the UN conference. "It is being killed by the very same people often thought to come to our rescue. No one is coming to our rescue."

BRITAIN'S BURNHAM BACKS RENEWABLES Earlier on Thursday, the leaders of small island states including the Bahamas, Tuvalu, the Solomon Islands and Saint Lucia called for swift action. "Major emitters must move beyond the usual promises. They must reduce emissions that the climate crisis demands," said Saint Lucia's Prime Minister Philip J . Pierre. British Prime Minister Andy Burnham backed a proposal by Turkey to increase electricity's share of world energy consumption to 35 per cent by 2035, from a little over a fifth now, to help advance that goal. Turkey has not specified whether the extra energy used would be renewable. Burnham told the conference that energy supply disruptions from the US-Israeli war with Iran and Russia's war with Ukraine showed clean energy was the wise choice. "It is now plain for everyone to see that if we depend on energy we do not control, then we leave ourselves exposed to prices we cannot control," he said. "The shift to clean energy is the only r out e to energy security." Developing countries reiterated requests that they have made during many years of UN talks for rich countries to provide more finance to help them shift to cleaner energy, adapt to a warming world , and repair climate-driven destruction. Fernanda de Carvalho, the head of climate policy for the World Wildlife Fund environmental group, said he found the leaders ' speeches underwhelming, especially as COP31 i s the first UN conference since scientists have publicly said the world is set to breach the 1.5C threshold. "It is worrying that the climate issue is not as high on the global political agenda as it needs to be," he said.
